# 1. Description of changes from the previous version and methodological approach

## 1.1 Changes and updates from the previous version

This is the second iteration of the review, please see the previously published and first iteration in [@siafis2024]. The same methodology was followed as the first iteration, and data from the updated search were incorporated.

There were the following changes compared to the previous version of the review:

1.  This document was restructured with clearer subcategories for the meta-analysis of the different comparisons and other sections to improve readability.
2.  No changes in the methodology (e.g., eligibility criteria, search strategies, data synthesis approach). However, we preferred to use the total score of the Brief Negative Symptom Scale (BNSS) to measure negative symptoms, rather than the subscales or subscores of the PANSS, based on recent studies suggesting that the BNSS is more suitable than older scales [@weigel2023]. Accordingly, comparison 6.1.13 was updated, but the findings remained unchanged.
3.  Data became available for three previously identified studies that had not been included in the analysis due to lack of data. These data were obtained from a full publication for [@milanovic2024], clinicaltrials.gov for [@hoffmann-laroche2024], or conference abstract for ([@otsukapharmaceuticaldevelopmentcommercializationinc2024]; [@sirs2024]). These provided data for new comparisons (i.e., adjunctive treatment to antipsychotics with TAAR1 agonists vs. placebo), additional outcomes (e.g., relapse), and longer-term timepoints. The respective analyses were updated accordingly. There were no new data for the primary outcome in adults with acute schizophrenia, but one additional study was terminated earlier [@sumitomo2024] but no data are available to be included in the analysis, thus, we assessed the potenital impact of the omission of this data in a sensitivty analysis (see 9.3).
4.  Two additional studies were identified in the updated searches: i) @pet_ralmitaront, a two-period crossover randomized trial examining ralmitaront 150 mg/day versus placebo, each administered for two weeks, in patients with clinically stable schizophrenia, assessing neuroimaging measures and safety— no data were available, ii) @otsuka_new an ongoing phase III double-blind randomized trial comparing ulotaront 75 mg/day, 150 mg/day, and placebo in individuals with acute schizophrenia over six weeks.
5.  Typos were corrected, and comparison 6.2.11 (dropouts due to adverse events) was revised, as dropouts due to any reason had been mistakenly reported instead of dropouts specifically due to adverse events.

## 1.2 Methodological approach

1.  We searched for all controlled and uncontrolled studies examining TAAR1 agonists. In the first and second iteration of the review, we analyzed usable data from all randomized controlled studies comparing any TAAR1 agonist to placebo or current antipsychotics in people with psychosis, other mental health conditions, or healthy volunteers. We did not include uncontrolled studies, except for mechanistic insights (see the extended data for additional explanations).

2.  We examined efficacy outcomes, including overall symptoms of psychosis (primary outcome) and symptom domains, dropouts due to any reason, and adverse events. Safety outcomes included death, serious adverse events, and specific adverse events. We also sought mechanistic outcomes, specifically neurobiological measures of dopaminergic, glutamatergic, and serotonergic signalling. We examined these outcomes at three time points: immediately after a single dose up to 2 weeks of treatment, 3-13 weeks of treatment (preferably at 6 weeks), and longer-term outcomes.

3.  In terms of efficacy outcomes, we pooled the data for each specific subgroup, considering that differences can be expected among different diagnoses (e.g., schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease psychosis) and patient subgroups (e.g., patients with an acute episode of schizophrenia or with predominant negative symptoms). In terms of other outcomes, we combined data from all subgroups but also presented data separately for each subgroup.

4.  Summary of data extraction: For continuous outcomes, we preferred change over endpoint scores and data from appropriate models or imputations considering missing outcome data. For dichotomous outcomes, we again preferred data from all participants, but in case of participants with missing outcome data, we assumed that they did not experience the event; an assumption usually used in meta-analysis in schizophrenia (e.g., @RN2). In terms of crossover studies, we preferred data from appropriate models considering period or carry-over effects. If not available, we assumed a correlation (i.e., 0.2 for adverse events) to correct the variance of the estimates according to @elbourne2002 . If an outcome was measured multiple times after a single dose of the drug, we calculated the area under the curve according to the linear trapezoid rule [@RN120] and divided by the time of assessment to remove the time component.

5.  Risk of bias was assessed using the RoB2 tool [@RN64] for parallel and crossover studies. When only one domain had some concerns, we assigned an overall low risk of bias. Otherwise, we used the worst judgment across domains.

6.  The effect sizes were as follows: 1) standardized mean differences (SMD) for efficacy outcomes, given that various scales have been used in the literature to allow comparability of the findings with other studies of antipsychotic drugs; 2) mean differences (MD) for laboratory measures, i.e., weight (kg), QTc interval (msec), and prolactin levels (ng/ml); 3) odds ratios (OR) for dichotomous outcomes, which were also converted to absolute risks using a control event rate [@RN71]. 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) are presented, but 95% prediction intervals are not presented due to the small number of studies. Other effect sizes were not used in the first and second iteration of the review, e.g., those used in meta-analysis of variance due to the paucity of data.

7.  Meta-analysis was conducted primarily using a random-effects model with inverse variance and REML estimator of tau-squared. Due to the small number of studies (\<5) in all analyses, we did not correct the confidence intervals using the Hartung-Knapp method [@RN82], and we also presented the findings from fixed-effects models using the Mantel-Haenszel method throughout. Meta-analysis of proportions was conducted to pool the control groups to estimate the control event rate using logit transformation of the proportions and inverse variance method [@schwarzer2019]. Moreover, continuity corrections of 0.5 were applied in case of 0 events in one of the groups.

8.  Sensitivity analysis of the primary outcome included using fixed-effect methods (*post-hoc* due to the small number of studies), restricting the analysis to studies with an overall low risk of bias, and excluding studies with imputed values. A *post-hoc* sensitivity analysis was also conducted in this iteration to examine the potential impact of omitting the findings of a prematurely terminated study [@sumitomo2024] on the summary effects of the primary outcome.

9.  Subgroup analyses and meta-regressions were not conducted due to the paucity of data. However, we explored potential dose-effects for the primary outcome by plotting the effect sizes for different fixed doses of TAAR1 agonists compared to placebo (while correcting for the use of common comparators [@higgins2019]).

10. Summary of evidence tables were constructed for all outcomes, including a summary of the association, within-study biases, across-study biases, biases due to indirectness, and other biases. We used the RoB2 tool [@RN64] to assess within-study biases, as mentioned above. We used the ROB-ME approach [@page2023] for evaluating biases in missing evidence and across-study biases. Indirectness was considered especially relevant for non-efficacy outcomes, where we pooled data across diagnoses and subgroups, and considered the percentage of studies and participants with schizophrenia, the main group for which this evidence would be applicable.

11. Finally, as there were no usable data from controlled experimental studies on the effects of TAAR1 agonists on neurobiological measures relevant to dopaminergic, serotonergic, or glutamatergic signalling, we could not analyze them as secondary outcomes in the current review. Nevertheless, to provide mechanistic insights, we narratively described the findings of any available mechanistic data from controlled and uncontrolled studies, irrespective of their inclusion in this review, given that we had comprehensively searched for them [@siafis2023]. We also presented the findings of these studies narratively in summary of evidence tables and discussed potential issues of risk of bias, reporting bias, indirectness, and other biases, but without formally using risk of bias tools.

*Please see the manuscript, extended data (*<https://osf.io/tdmau/>*), the protocol [@siafis2023] and the publication of the first iteration [@siafis2024] for more details.*

*A list of abbreviations can be find towards the end of the document.*

**We present below the results, including the PRISMA flow diagram [@page2021] , table of included studies, risk of bias assessment, and forest plots, to facilitate a better understanding of the summary of evidence tables and the manuscript. Please refer to the detailed description of the findings in the latter part of the manuscript for more information.**

# 4. Description of included studies

There were 27 eligible studies, which characteristics can be found in **Table 1**, with 25 studies (2826 participants) being completed and 3 studies being still ongoing (according to the status reported in clinicaltrials.gov up to 12.08.2025).

The studies used to describe mechanistic insights are provided in the relevant section below. It should be noted that the findings from an additional single-arm molecular neuroimaging are described in this section [@RN132], which was uncontrolled and formally excluded from this iteration of the review. The characteristics of this study and its findings are described in the "mechanistic insights" section.

## 4.1 Completed studies with usable data

There were usable data for this analysis from 12 studies (2175 participants) [@RN116; @RN13; @RN110; @RN111; @RN112; @RN113; @RN115; @RN123; @RN124; @milanovic2024; @nct04115319; @hoffmann-laroche2024], which enrolled adult populations across multiple countries and were funded by the industry manufacturing the TAAR1 agonists.

### 4.1.1 Studies examining multiple doses of TAAR1 agonists

The usable studies compared single or multiple doses of two TAAR1 agonists (i.e., ulotaront or ralmitaront) with placebo or current antipsychotics (i.e., prior antipsychotics, risperidone, amisulpride or quetiapine) in people with schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease psychosis, other mental health conditions (narcolepsy/cateplexy as sleep disorder) and healthy volunteers.

*Seven studies* used a parallel design to examine the efficacy and safety of multiple doses of TAAR1 agonists in psychosis within 3-13 weeks (six studies) and \>13 weeks (1 study):

-   *Four studies* examining daily doses of TAAR1 agonists in adults with an acute episode of schizophrenia spectrum conditions for 4-6 weeks, 3 examined ulotaront [@RN110; @RN111; @RN112] and 1 examined ralmitaront [@RN113]. These studies used placebo as a control group, and the 1 study on ralmitaront also used the antipsychotic risperidone as an active comparator.

-   *One study* compared ralmitaront as monotherapy or as an adjunct to antipsychotics in adults with schizophrenia spectrum conditions and negative symptoms for 12 weeks [@hoffmann-laroche2024].

-   *One study* comparing daily doses of ulotaront in Parkinson's disease psychosis to placebo for 4 weeks [@RN13].

-   *One study* used a parallel design to examine the efficacy and safety of multiple doses of TAAR1 agonists in psychosis for more than 13 weeks, specifically comparing ulotaront with quetiapine in adults with clinically-stable schizophrenia for 52 weeks [@nct04115319].

### 4.1.2 Studies examining single doses of TAAR1 agonists

*Five studies* examined the pharmacokinetics, safety and/or neuroimaging of single doses of TAAR1 agonists or multiple doses for up to 2 weeks:

-   *One study* examining the effects of a single dose of 150mg ulotaront in clinically stable adults with schizophrenia on QTc interval within a day [@RN124]. The study utilized a three-period crossover period comparing ulotaront with placebo and moxifloxacin (an antibiotic used as active comparator, not relevant for our analysis).

-   *Two studies* examined the effects of single doses of ulotaront in healthy volunteers on sleep parameters [@RN116] or fMRI tasks [@RN115]. @RN116 included two cohorts of crossover studies comparing two single doses of ulotaront with placebo. [@RN115] was a parallel trial comparing ulotaront to placebo or the antipsychotic amisulpride on fMRI tasks relevant to reward, working memory and emotion processing in volunteers with high or low schizotypy traits.

-   *One study* examined two single doses of ulotaront in adults with narcolepsy-cateplexy compared to placebo using a three-period crossover design [@RN123].

-   *One study* examined the effects of a single dose of ulotaront compared to previous antipsychotics (aripiprazole, olanzapine, risperidone or quetiapine) in adults with schizophrenia and concurrent metabolic syndrome on gastric emptying using a crossover design [@milanovic2024].

## 4.2 Completed studies with unavailable data

Data from the following studies were unavailable:

-   *One study* examined the efficacy and safety of ulotaront in comparison to placebo in adolescents with an acute episode schizophrenia (NCT04072354). This study had two parts with adults and adolescents. This study has been recently completed, and although some usable data in the adult population are available (see above), these are not available for the adolescents.

-   *One study* examined the efficacy and safety of two ulotaront doses of 50mg/d and 75mg/d in comparison to placebo in 83 adults with an acute episode of schizophrenia (NCT04825860). The study was terminated early in 2023-10.

-   *One study* had a crossover, double-blind design and examined the safety and neuroimaging effects of ralmitaront 150 mg/day compared to placebo over two weeks of treatment in 35 adults with clinically stable schizophrenia (NCT06880328). The study was completed in September 2019 but was retrospectively registered in March 202.

-   *Nine studies* examined pharmacokinetics and safety of single or few multiple doses of ulotaront or ralmitaront in healthy volunteers (Fowler 2015, JapicCTI-194581, NCT02699372, SEP361-101, DA801002, NCT01940159, Koblan 2016, NCT04325737, NCT04865835).

## 4.3 Ongoing studies

The following studies are ongoing:

-   *One study* is examining the efficacy and safety of ulotaront 75 mg/day and 100 mg/day compared to placebo in 522 adults with acute schizophrenia (NCT06894212). The trial is expected to be completed in 2028.
-   *Two studies* are examining the efficacy and safety of ulotaront compared to placebo in other mental health conditions, i.e., adults with major depression (NCT05593029) and generalized anxiety disorder (NCT05729373). These trials are expected to be completed in 2025-2026, and their safety data are relevant for this review.

# 5. Risk of bias assessment

The risk of bias of the studies was examined using the RoB2 tool [@RN64] for parallel and crossover studies for all outcomes. Here, we present the risk of bias of using the worst judgement of a domain across outcomes. It should be noted that when there were some concerns in only one of the domains, we assigned an overall low risk of bias according to our protocol.

```{r echo =F, fig.fullwidth=T, fig.width=7.2, fig.height=6}
rob_traffic_light(rob_all, tool="Generic")
```

**Figure 2** Risk of bias of studies with usable data

All the studies were double-blind randomized controlled studies, with a low risk of bias in most cases in their respective domains of biases due to randomization, deviations from intended interventions, and outcome measurement. An exception was one open-label crossover study examining a single dose of ulotaront versus previous antipsychotics [@milanovic2024]. There were also no indications of selectively reported results; thus, the studies had a low risk of bias in their respective domains. Most of the studies had missing outcome data, but there was no clear indication that the missingness depended on the true value of the effects for most of the outcomes. Therefore, there were some concerns, except for [@RN13; @hoffmann-laroche2024; @nct04115319] , which had a high risk of bias for efficacy outcomes but not for adverse events and other outcomes. Additionally, there were few differences in this domain across outcomes, such as a low risk for the outcome of dropouts. In terms of the four crossover studies, there was a low risk of bias in period and carry-over effects, except for some concerns in the three-period crossover study of @RN124 and the open-label crossover study of @milanovic2024. Few differences across outcomes can be found in the overall judgment of the risk of bias for each study per outcome in the respective forest plots below.

# 6. Results for the comparisons

**It should be noted that the x-axis in the figures below, which present dichotomous outcomes using odds ratios, is logarithmically scaled.** **When the forest plots present only the effect sizes, there were crossover studies in which variances were corrected assuming a correlation of 0.2.**

## 6.1 *TAAR1 agonist* vs *placebo (monotherapy)*

This section refers to the comparson of TAAR1 agonists versus placebo as monotherapy. See comparison 6.3 for TAAR1 agonists versus placebo as adjunctive treatment to antipsychotics.

Furthermore, there were narrative descriptions from a conference abstract [@RN109] that ulotaront did not differ from placebo in extrapyramidal symptoms with low absolute frequencies in two unpublished phase III trials [@RN111; @RN112]. Moreover, ulotaront was reported not to deteriorate movement symptoms in participants with Parkinson's disease psychosis as measured with the Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale Part III [@RN13].

### 6.1.32 Summary outcome plots

#### Efficacy outcomes

```{r echo=F, fig.fullwidth=T, fig.width=12, fig.height=5, warning=FALSE}

outcome_categories<-outcome_names %>% 
  select(outcome, event_text) 

efficacy_primary<-meta_outcome %>% left_join(outcome_categories) %>% 
  filter(outcome=="cognition" | outcome=="depression" | outcome=="negative" | outcome=="overall" | outcome=="positive") %>% #efficacy outcome
  filter(!is.na(TE.random)) %>% filter(!is.na(event_text)) %>%
  mutate(point=TE.random,
         lb=TE.random-1.96*seTE.random,
         ub=TE.random+1.96*seTE.random) %>% 
  unique() %>%
  filter(comparison=="taar1_vs_placebo") %>% 
  mutate(n_text=paste0("N=", k,", n=",n))

efficacy_primary$population <- factor(efficacy_primary$population, levels=unique(efficacy_primary$population))
efficacy_primary$event_text <- factor(efficacy_primary$event_tex, levels=unique(efficacy_primary$event_tex))
level_outcomes<- c("Overall symptoms", "Positive symptoms", "Negative symptoms", "Depressive symptoms", "Cognitive impairement")
level_population<-c("Schizophrenia spectrum (acute episode)","Schizophrenia spectrum (negative symptoms)", "Parkinson Disease Psychosis")

ggplot(data=efficacy_primary, 
       aes(y=factor(event_text, level=rev(level_outcomes)), x=point))+
  geom_text(aes(x=0.65, label=n_text), colour="black" , position=position_dodge(width = 0.9))+
  geom_point(aes(size=n), position=position_dodge(width = 0.5), colour="royalblue4")+ #Size proportional to the number of participants
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(-0.8,0.8))+
  geom_errorbar(aes(x=point, xmin=lb, 
                    xmax=ub),
                width=0, position=position_dodge(width = 0.5), colour="royalblue4")+
  scale_size_continuous(guide=FALSE)+
  geom_vline(xintercept=0, linetype='dashed')+
  facet_grid(~factor(population, levels=level_population))+
  ylab("")+
  xlab("SMD 95%CI (SMD>0: TAAR1 agonist better)")+
  theme_bw()


```

**Figure 40** Summary plot for efficacy outcomes at 4-6 weeks for the comparison of TAAR1 agonists vs. placebo in the three populations of patients with an acute episode of schizophrenia, schizophrenia and negative symptoms and Parkinson's disease psychosis. There were only available data for the timepoint of 3-13 weeks. The size of the points are proportional to the number of participants used in the analysis. SMD\>0 correspond to more symptom improvement by TAAR1 agonists compared to placebo. The findings of the random-effects model are presented. SMD: Standardized mean difference, 95%CI: 95% confidence interval. N=number of studies, n=number of participants.

It should be noted that there were also data for relapse that are not displayed in this figure (see instead 2.5.9).

#### Dropouts and side-effects

```{r echo=F, fig.fullwidth=T, fig.width=11, fig.height=12, warning=FALSE}
safety_primary<-meta_outcome %>% left_join(ae_categories) %>%  #I need to change a bit 
  mutate(event_text=ifelse(outcome=="death", "Mortality", 
                           ifelse(outcome=="serious", "Serious event", 
                                  ifelse(outcome=="dropout_any", "Dropouts any reason",
                                         ifelse(outcome=="dropout_ae", "Dropouts adverse event", event_text)))),
         MedDRA_group=ifelse(outcome=="death" | outcome=="serious", "serious",
                             ifelse(outcome=="dropout_any" | outcome=="dropout_ae", "dropouts", MedDRA_group))) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(TE.random)) %>% filter(!is.na(event_text)) %>%
  mutate(point=TE.random,
         lb=TE.random-1.96*seTE.random,
         ub=TE.random+1.96*seTE.random) %>% unique() %>%
  filter(comparison=="taar1_vs_placebo") %>% 
  mutate(n_text=paste0("N=", k,", n=",n))

safety_primary_plot <-safety_primary

safety_primary_plot$event_text <- factor(safety_primary_plot$event_tex, levels=unique(safety_primary_plot$event_tex))
level_order<- sort(unique(safety_primary_plot$event_text))
lever_order_meddra<-c("dropouts", "any", "serious", "autonomic", "endocrinic", "neuromuscular", "neuropsychiatric")

safety_primary_plot$event_text <- factor(safety_primary_plot$event_tex, levels=unique(safety_primary_plot$event_tex))
level_order<- sort(unique(safety_primary_plot$event_text))
lever_order_meddra<-c("dropouts", "any", "serious", "autonomic", "endocrinic", "neuromuscular", "neuropsychiatric")

safety_primary_plot$timepoint <- factor(safety_primary_plot$timepoint, 
                                        levels = c("1 day-2 weeks", "3-13 weeks", ">13 weeks"))


safety_primary_plot<-safety_primary_plot %>% mutate(type_outcome=ifelse(outcome=="dropout_any" | outcome=="dropout_ae", "dropout", "side"))

ggplot(data=safety_primary_plot, 
       aes(y=factor(event_text, level=rev(level_order)), x=exp(point),colour=type_outcome, shape=timepoint))+
  geom_text(aes(x=0.03, label=n_text), colour="black" , position=position_dodge(width = 0.9))+
  geom_point(aes(size=n), position=position_dodge(width = 0.5))+
  geom_errorbar(aes(x=exp(point), xmin=exp(TE.random-1.96*seTE.random), 
                    xmax=exp(TE.random+1.96*seTE.random), colour=type_outcome,shape=timepoint),
                width=0, position=position_dodge(width = 0.5))+
  geom_vline(xintercept=1, linetype='dashed')+
  scale_size_continuous(guide=FALSE)+
  facet_grid(factor(MedDRA_group, levels=lever_order_meddra)~., scales = "free", space = "free")+
  scale_x_log10() +
  ylab("")+
  scale_shape_manual(values=c(1, 19, 17))+
  scale_colour_manual(guide=FALSE, values=c("green4", "firebrick4"))+
  xlab("OR 95%CI (OR>1: TAAR1 agonists worse)")+
  theme_bw()


```

**Figure 41** Summary forest plot for dropouts and side-effects for the comparison of TAAR1 agonists compared to placebo and for the two timepoints with usable data. It should be noted that different populations have been pooled in the analysis of dropouts and adverse events including schizophrenia (acute phase, negative symptoms), Parkinson's disease psychosis, narcolepsy-cateplexy and healthy volunteers. The size is proportional to the number of participants in the analysis. The findings of the random-effects model are presented. OR\>1 corresponds to more events with TAAR1 agonists compared to placebo. OR: Odds ratio, 95%CI: 95% confidence intervals. N=number of studies, n=number of participants.

## 6.2 *TAAR1 agonist* vs *antipsychotic (monotherapy)*

### 6.2.1 Overall symptoms (primary outcome)

#### Timepoint 1: *1 day - 2 weeks*

No usable data available from RCT.

#### Timepoint 2: *3 weeks - 13 weeks*

```{r echo=F, fig.fullwidth=T, fig.width=12, fig.height=4}

       col.diamond = "royalblue4",
       col.square =   "royalblue1",
                 rightcols = c("effect", "ci","Overall"),

```

### 6.2.32 Summary outcome plots

#### Efficacy outcomes

```{r echo=F, fig.fullwidth=T, fig.width=10, fig.height=5, warning=FALSE}

outcome_categories<-outcome_names %>% 
  select(outcome, event_text) 

efficacy_primary_2<-meta_outcome %>% left_join(outcome_categories) %>% 
  filter(outcome=="cognition" | outcome=="depression" | outcome=="negative" | outcome=="overall" | outcome=="positive" ) %>% #efficacy outcome
  filter(!is.na(TE.random)) %>% filter(!is.na(event_text)) %>%
  mutate(point=TE.random,
         lb=TE.random-1.96*seTE.random,
         ub=TE.random+1.96*seTE.random) %>% 
  unique() %>%
  filter(comparison=="taar1_vs_antipsychotic") %>% 
  mutate(n_text=paste0("N=", k,", n=",n))

efficacy_primary_2$population <- factor(efficacy_primary_2$population, levels=unique(efficacy_primary_2$population))
efficacy_primary_2$event_text <- factor(efficacy_primary_2$event_tex, levels=unique(efficacy_primary_2$event_tex))
level_outcomes<- c("Overall symptoms", "Positive symptoms", "Negative symptoms", "Depressive symptoms", "Cognitive impairement")
level_population<-c("Schizophrenia spectrum")

ggplot(data=efficacy_primary_2, 
       aes(y=factor(event_text, level=rev(level_outcomes)), x=point))+
  geom_text(aes(x=0.65, label=n_text), colour="black" , position=position_dodge(width = 0.9))+
  geom_point(size=3.4,position=position_dodge(width = 0.5), colour="royalblue4")+ #Size proportional to the number of participants
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(-0.8,0.8))+
  geom_errorbar(aes(x=point, xmin=lb, 
                    xmax=ub),
                width=0, position=position_dodge(width = 0.5), colour="royalblue4")+
  scale_size_continuous(guide=FALSE)+
  geom_vline(xintercept=0, linetype='dashed')+
  facet_grid(~factor(population))+ #levels=level_population))+
  ylab("")+
  xlab("SMD 95%CI (SMD>0: TAAR1 agonists better)")+
  theme_bw()


```

**Figure 76** Summary plot for efficacy outcomes at 4 weeks for the comparison of TAAR1 agonists versus antipscyhotcs in patients with an acute episode of schizophrenia. There were only data for the timepoint of 3-13 weeks. There were only data for ralmitaront as TAAR1 agonist and risperidone as control group. SMD\>0 correspond to more symptom improvement by TAAR1 agonists compared to antipsychotic. SMD: Standardized mean difference, 95%CI: 95% confidence interval. N=number of studies, n=number of participants.

It should be noted that there were also data for relapse that are not displayed in this figure (see instead 2.6.9).

#### Dropouts and side-effects

```{r echo=F, fig.fullwidth=T, fig.width=11, fig.height=12, warning=FALSE}
safety_primary_2<-meta_outcome %>% left_join(ae_categories) %>%  
  mutate(event_text=ifelse(outcome=="death", "Mortality", 
                           ifelse(outcome=="serious", "Serious event", 
                                  ifelse(outcome=="dropout_any", "Dropouts any reason",
                                         ifelse(outcome=="dropout_ae", "Dropouts adverse event", event_text)))),
         MedDRA_group=ifelse(outcome=="death" | outcome=="serious", "serious",
                             ifelse(outcome=="dropout_any" | outcome=="dropout_ae", "dropouts", MedDRA_group))) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(TE.random)) %>% filter(!is.na(event_text)) %>%
  mutate(point=TE.random,
         lb=TE.random-1.96*seTE.random,
         ub=TE.random+1.96*seTE.random) %>% unique() %>%
  filter(comparison=="taar1_vs_antipsychotic") %>% 
  mutate(n_text=paste0("N=", k,", n=",n))

safety_primary_plot_2 <-safety_primary_2

safety_primary_plot_2$event_text <- factor(safety_primary_plot_2$event_tex, levels=unique(safety_primary_plot_2$event_tex))
level_order_2<- sort(unique(safety_primary_plot_2$event_text))
lever_order_meddra<-c("dropouts", "any", "serious", "autonomic", "endocrinic", "neuromuscular", "neuropsychiatric")

safety_primary_plot_2<-safety_primary_plot_2 %>% mutate(type_outcome=ifelse(outcome=="dropout_any" | outcome=="dropout_ae", "dropout", "side"))

safety_primary_plot_2$timepoint <- factor(safety_primary_plot_2$timepoint, 
                                        levels = c("1 day-2 weeks", "3-13 weeks", ">13 weeks"))


ggplot(data=safety_primary_plot_2, 
       aes(y=factor(event_text, level=rev(level_order_2)), x=exp(point),colour=type_outcome, shape=timepoint))+
  geom_text(aes(x=0.01, label=n_text), colour="black" , position=position_dodge(width = 0.9))+
  geom_point(aes(size=n), position=position_dodge(width = 0.5))+
  geom_errorbar(aes(x=exp(point), xmin=exp(TE.random-1.96*seTE.random), 
                    xmax=exp(TE.random+1.96*seTE.random), colour=type_outcome,shape=timepoint),
                width=0, position=position_dodge(width = 0.5))+
  geom_vline(xintercept=1, linetype='dashed')+
  scale_size_continuous(guide=FALSE, range=c(1,3))+
  facet_grid(factor(MedDRA_group, levels=lever_order_meddra)~., scales = "free", space = "free")+
  scale_x_log10() +
  ylab("")+
  scale_shape_manual(values=c(1, 19, 17))+
  scale_colour_manual(guide=FALSE, values=c("green4", "firebrick4"))+
  xlab("OR 95%CI (OR>1: TAAR1 agonists worse)")+
  theme_bw()



```

**Figure 77** Summary forest plot for dropouts and side-effects for the comparison of TAAR1 agonists compared to antipsychotics and for the three timepoints with usable data. There were data for single doses of ulotaront versus amisulpride in healthy volunteers at 1 day, single dose of ulotaront versus previous antipsychotic in adults with schizophrenia and concurrent metabolic syndrome at 1 day, ralmitaront versus risperidone in acute schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder at 4 weeks, ulotaront versus quetiapine in clinically stable adults with schizophrenia at 52 weeks. The size of the points is proportional to the number of participants. OR\>1 corresponds to more events with TAAR1 agonists compared to antipsychotics. OR: Odds ratio, 95%CI: 95% confidence interval. N=number of studies, n=number of participants.

# 7. Mechanistic insights into the effects of TAAR1 agonism for psychosis

In the first version of the review, there were no usable data available from RCTs on neurobiological measures relevant to psychosis and neurotransmitter signalling that could be analyzed as secondary outcomes of this review. Therefore, to be able to provide additional insights into the mechanism of TAAR1 agonism for psychosis, we sought to describe any potentially available data from both controlled and uncontrolled studies, irrespective of whether they have been included or not in the review (see above).

In the second version of the review, we also identified one crossover RCT that examined the effects of ralmitaront 150 mg/day versus placebo on neuroimaging measures in individuals with clinically stable schizophrenia [@pet_ralmitaront] . However, no data or results from this trial, which was retrospectively registered and had not been identified in our previous version or searches, were available.

Additional evidence from two neuroimaging studies [@RN115; @RN132] generally supports the notion that TAAR1 agonists can ameliorate the elevated striatal dopamine synthesis and release capacity that is considered central in the development of symptoms of psychosis [@howes2022].

## 7.1 Evidence from functional neuroimaging

Two studies were available:

-   @RN115 was double-blind, three-arm parallel RCT examining the effects of a single dose of ulotaront 50mg compared to placebo and amisulpride 400mg on fMRI blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) striatal responses to reward processing, as measured during the anticipation phase of the Monetary Incentive Delay (MID) task (primary outcome). BOLD striatal responses to reward during the anticipatory phase of MID were selected as the primary outcome due to their potential relation to increased dopamine release in the striatum. The study enrolled 96 healthy volunteers, 51 with low schizotypy traits and 45 with high, as measured with the Schizotypal Personality Questionnaire (scores \<10 indicate low schizotypy traits, \>=40 high schizotypy traits) to examine interactions due to the potential shared increased striatal activity between positive symptoms and schizotypal traits. The interventions were administered 2 hours before the fMRI. Moreover, the study measured responses to other brain regions, the outcome phase of MID, BOLD responses to the N-back task for working memory, responses to an emotional test battery, resting state connectivity, and arterial spin labelling.

    The findings of the primary outcome of this study are reported here as they were deemed most relevant to dopaminergic signalling:

    -   Ulotaront appeared to be associated with smaller BOLD striatal responses compared to placebo (left striatum: -0.13%, p=0.03, SMD=-0.55, 95%CI: -1.05, -0.05; right striatum: -0.12%, p=0.06, SMD=-0.44, 95%CI: -0.94, 0.06) but not to amisulpride (left: -0.07%, p=0.38, SMD=-0.22, 95%CI: -0.71, 0.27; right: -0.03%, p=0.66, SMD: -0.11, 95%CI: -0.60, 0.38) in the anticipation of loss, and did not differ from both placebo (left: -0.07%, p=0.30, SMD=-0.25, 95%CI: -0.75, 0.25; right: -0.07%, p=0.27, SMD=-0.25, 95%CI: -0.75, 0.25) and amisulpride (left: -0.03%, p=0.65, SMD=-0.11, 95%CI: -0.60, 0.38; right: -0.02%, p=0.74, SMD=-0.08, 95%CI: -0.57, 0.41) in the anticipation of win in the MID task.

    -   There were no differences in BOLD insular responses (anticipation of loss - ulotaront vs. placebo left 0.00%, p=0.99, SMD=0.00, 95%CI: -0.50, 0.50 and right -0.10%, p=0.16 SMD=-0.36, 95%CI:-0.86, 0.14. ulotaront vs. amisulpride left 0.01%, p=0.94, SMD=0.02, 95%CI: -0.48, 0.52 and right -0.08%, p=0.42, SMD=-0.20, 95%CI: -0.70, 0.30; anticipation of win - ulotaront vs. placebo left: 0.08%, p=0.18, SMD=0.34, 95%CI: -0.16, 0.84, and right -0.01%, p=0.90, SMD=-0.04, 95%CI: -0.54, 0.46, ulotaront vs. amisulpride left 0.02%, p=0.84, SMD=0.05, 95%CI: -0.45, 0.55, and right 0.03%, p=0.72, SMD=0.09, 95%CI: -0.40, 0.58).

    -   Ulotaront seemed to increase BOLD responses in the medial orbital frontal cortex in anticipation of loss compared to placebo (left: 0.19%, p=0.07, SMD=0.44, 95%CI: -0.06, 0.94; right: 0.17%, p=0.10, SMD=0.43, 95%CI: -0.07, 0.93) and amisulpride (left: 0.25%, p=0.03, SMD=0.56, 95%CI: 0.06, 1.06; right: 0.22%, p=0.05, SMD=0.50, 95%CI: 0.00, 1.00) and in anticipation of win compared to placebo (left: 0.25%, p=0.01, SMD=0.64, 95%CI: 0.14, 1.14; right: 0.24%, p=0.01, SMD=0.68, 95%CI: 0.18, 1.18), but not clearly to amisulpride (left: 0.10%, p=0.30, SMD=0.26, 95%CI: -0.24, 0.76; right: 0.11%, p=0.19, SMD=0.33, 95%CI: -0.16, 0.82).

    -   Interactions with schizotypy traits were not reported for the primary outcome, but ulotaront was reported to reverse in comparison to placebo the aberrant increased BOLD response in the right insula observed in participants with high schizotypy traits but not in those with low schizotypy traits.

    However, it is unclear if the primary outcome was selected *a priori* or *a posteriori*, as no primary outcome was reported in the registration of the study on clinicaltrials.gov, thus biases due to seletected reported outcomes cannot be excluded. There were also differences between the interventions in some of the other measures, with ulotaront being reported as associated with the modification of signals in brain regions associated with cognitive symptoms in schizophrenia. Moreover, ulotaront was associated with sedation in 60% of the participants, more frequently than placebo (see **Figure 37**) and amisulpride (see **Figure 67**) that impaired reaction times in the tasks but was not correlated with BOLD responses. Nevertheless, the impact of this sedative effect on these findings is unclear.

    In conclusion, this study suggests that ulotaront might be able to reduce dopamine release in situations that are increased, like the anticipatory phase of MID, and potentially in psychosis.

-   @pet_ralmitaront was a double-blind crossover RCT comparing ralmitaront 150 mg/day versus placebo, each administered for two weeks, in 35 individuals with clinically stable schizophrenia. The trial used fMRI meaures including MID, but it was retrospectively registered and no results were available

## 7.2 Evidence from molecular neuroimaging

Two studies were available:

-   @RN132 was an open-label single-arm trial examining the effects of a 2-week treatment with ulotaront (50-75mg/d) as an add-on to antipsychotic treatment on dopamine synthesis capacity in clinically stable patients with schizophrenia (an uncontrolled study that was not included in this meta-analysis, with available data from a conference abstract in ACNPC 2024 [@RN109]). This study included 14 men and 5 women (aged 18-45 years, mean age 32.9 years) with clinically stable schizophrenia (DSM-5) on a stable dose of antipsychotics for at least 3 weeks before screening. Three additional patients were enrolled but did not complete the baseline scan, so they were excluded from the study. The patients underwent an F-DOPA PET scan both at baseline and after 2 weeks of treatment with ulotaront (50-75mg/d) as an add-on to antipsychotic treatment. At baseline, the patients had a mean PANSS total score of 79.3 (SD=7.3), PANSS positive subscale of 19.2 (SD=4.6), PANSS Marder positive factor of 24.3 (SD=4.6), and CGI-S of 4.2 (SD=0.6), indicating that the patients had on average symptoms of moderate severity.

    After 2 weeks of treatment with add-on ulotaront, there was a decrease in dopamine synthesis capacity in the striatum as indicated by the F-DOPA PET scan by -3.98% from baseline (95% CI: -8.68%, 0.72%), with the 95% CI not excluding the null effect, and the striatal subregions ranging from -3.38% in the associative striatum, -3.89% in the sensorimotor striatum, to -5.79% in the limbic striatum. This reduction was considered to be clinically meaningful, and although it was not correlated with the relative reduction in PANSS total scores (r=0.19, p\>0.05), it was correlated with improvements in the PANSS Marder positive factor (r=0.49, p\<0.05).

    The study can be considered to have a high risk of bias due to the single-arm design, lack of control conditions, and the absence of blinding, yet the measurement of dopamine synthesis capacity can be considered objective.

    In conclusion, this study suggests that ulotaront may be able to reduce the dopamine synthesis capacity in clinically stable, but still symptomatic, people with schizophrenia, and the decrease in dopamine synthesis could be associated with the improvement of symptoms.

-   @pet_ralmitaront was a double-blind crossover RCT comparing ralmitaront 150 mg/day versus placebo, each administered for two weeks, in 35 individuals with clinically stable schizophrenia. The trial measured F-DOPA signal in the striatum, but it was retrospectively registered and no results were available.

## 7.3 Other data

No other controlled or uncontrolled study (see *included and excluded studies* in the supplementary files of the review) reported any neurobiological measure. It should be noted that another study, i.e., NCT02699372, consisting of double-blind trials examining single and multiple ascending doses of ralmitaront compared to placebo in healthy volunteers (see *Table 1*), utilized neuropsychological tasks but did not couple them with neuroimaging or other neurobiological measures to provide further insights. There were no usable data for this study for any of the outcomes; only brief and narrative descriptions of the findings of these tasks were available in the study protocol of the ralmitaront acute phase study [@RN113]. These findings describe that ralmitaront improved reward-related behavioral tasks compared to placebo but lacked additional information.

# 8. Subgroup analyses and meta-regressions

## 8.1 Predefined subgroup analyses and meta-regressions

There were fewer than 5 studies available for the analyses of the primary outcome, precluding the exploration of potential reasons for heterogeneity with subgroup analyses and meta-regressions, such as age, sex, baseline severity, diagnosis and patient subgroups (see 8.2), the type of TAAR1 agonist (see 8.3, 8.4), the dose (see 8.4), and other characteristics of TAAR1 agonists.

## 8.2 Subgroups of participants

We presented the effect sizes in each specific subgroup of participants for all outcomes, but we did not perform a formal subgroup test.

## 8.3 Differences between ulotaront and ralmitaront

We explored potential differences between ulotaront and ralmitaront in improving overall symptoms of acute schizophrenia, but we did not conduct any formal subgroup test due to the limited number of studies.

```{r echo=F, fig.fullwidth=T, fig.width=12, fig.height=4}
forest(meta_comp_drug, 
       col.diamond = "royalblue4",
       col.square =   "royalblue1",
                 rightcols = c("effect", "ci","Overall"), 
                 rightlabs = c("SMD", "95%-CI", "Risk of bias"),  
       xlim=c(-0.8,0.8),
                 label.e = unique(meta_comp_drug$data$treat1_new), 
       label.c=unique(meta_comp_drug$data$treat2_new),
                 subgroup.hetstat = TRUE, overall.hetstat =FALSE, test.subgroup.random = FALSE,test.subgroup.fixed = FALSE,
                 overall = FALSE, prediction.subgroup = FALSE,
                 subgroup = TRUE, fixed=TRUE,
                 label.left = "Placebo better", label.right="TAAR1 better")
```

**Figure 94** Forest plot presenting the effects of ulotaront and ralmitaront compared to placebo on overall symptoms in acute schizophrenia (measured with PANSS total) at 4-6 weeks separately. SMD: Standardized mean difference, 95%CI: 95% confidence intervals, SD: standard deviation.

## 8.4 Dose-effect relationships

We explored potential dose-effects by plotting the effect sizes for each fixed-dose level of TAAR1 agonist compared to placebo in improving symptoms in acute schizophrenia (see 8.4.1) or in participants with schizophrenia and predominant negative symptoms (see 8.4.2). However, we did not conduct any formal subgroup test or dose-response meta-analysis due to the limited number of studies

#### 8.4.1 Exploration of dose-efffect of ulotaront and ralmitaront on overall symptoms of acute schizophrenia

```{r echo=F, fig.fullwidth=T, fig.width=11, fig.height=4, warning=FALSE}
ggplot(data=data_doses[data_doses$population=="acute",], aes(x=dose,
                                 y=-yi,
                                 ymin=-yi+1.96*sqrt(vi), ymax=-yi-1.96*sqrt(vi), 
                                 group=study_name, colour=study_name))+
  geom_pointrange(position=position_dodge(width = 1.2), aes(shape=schedule), size=1)+
  xlim(c(0,150))+
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(-0.8,0.8), expand=TRUE)+
  xlab("dose (mg//d)")+
  ylab("SMD 95%CI (SMD>0: TAAR1 agonists better)")+
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(15,0))+
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype="dashed")+
  facet_wrap(~drug_name,  scales = "free", nrow=2)+
  theme_bw()
```

**Figure 95** Effect sizes for each dose level of ulotaront and ralmitaront compared to placebo in improving overall symptoms of acute schizophrenia at 4-6 weeks are presented separately. The findings of each study are presented separately, and the effect sizes were corrected for using the same control condition in each study. It should be noted that @RN110 was a two-arm flexible-dosing study, and its effect size is placed in the middle of the range of the administered dose (50mg/d to 75mg/d). SMD: Standardized mean difference, 95%CI: 95% confidence intervals.

In the fixed-dosing studies [@RN111; @RN112; @RN113], higher doses (i.e., ulotaront 100mg/d and ralmitaront 150mg/d) may be associated with more improvement compared to smaller doses. However, the effect sizes at these high doses still appear to be small, with a standardized mean difference (SMD) of approximately 0.2. In the flexible dosing study by @RN110 , which utilized doses of ulotaront up to 75mg/d, small-to-medium effect sizes were observed. Importantly, the available data are limited. Moreover, another study [@sumitomo2024] examined two fixed-doses of ulotaront (50 mg/d and 75 mg/d) compared to placebo, but it is still unpublished with no data available, and it was terminated earlier due to company business strategy. Therefore, dose-effect findings are inconclusive.


**Figure 96** Effect sizes for each dose level of ralmitaront compared to placebo (monotherapy or add-on to antipsychotic treamtnet) in improving overall symptoms (measured with PANSS total; primary outcome) and negative symptoms (measured with BNSS) in people with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and predominant negative symptoms in at 12 weeks. The findings of each part of the single available study of @hoffmann-laroche2024 (part A for monotherapy and part B for add-on treatment) are presented separately, and the effect sizes were corrected for using the same control condition in each study. In this exploratory analysis, we focused on negative symptom scores rather than overall symptoms (primary outcome of the review).

It appeared that ralmitaront 45 mg/d, which was examined as an add-on treatment, resulted potentially in a worsening of overall symptoms and smaller reduction in negative symptoms compared to the higher doses of 150 mg/d and 300 mg/d; this study arm included 5 participants and it was discontinued. The available data were limited, and the findings remained inconclusive.

# 9. Sensitivity analyses

## 9.1. Predefined sensitivity analyses

We did not conduct the following predefined sensitivity analyses for the primary outcome due to the limited data:

1.  Restricting the analysis to studies with low risk of bias, since there were 4 studies with low risk of bias in acute schizophrenia [@RN110; @RN111; @RN112; @RN113], 1 study with high risk of bias in Parkinson's disease psychosis (1 study with high risk of bias) [@RN13] and 1 study with high risk of bias in schizophrenia and negative symptoms [@hoffmann-laroche2024].

2.  Excluding imputed data, since no imputed data were used in the analysis of the primary outcome. There were no imputed data in the analysis of the primary outcome.

## 9.2 Random- and fixed-effects meta-analysis

Due to the limited number of studies, we also presented a fixed-effects model for all outcomes in addition to the random-effects model to assess the robustness of the findings. The findings were robust in the majority of cases. For the primary outcome in the meta-analysis of 4 studies in acute schizophrenia [@RN110; @RN111; @RN112; @RN113], the point estimate of the effect sizes did not differ between random- and fixed-effects (SMD:0.15 and 0.13, respectively), but the 95% CI in the fixed-effects model was narrower, excluding the null effect (95% CI: -0.05, 0.34, and 0.02, 0.25, respectively). Nonetheless, the interpretation of the findings that TAAR1 agonists have little to no effect compared to placebo in improving overall symptoms does not change

## 9.3 Exploration of the impact of potentially omitted results

This post-hoc sensitivity analysis was conducted to assess whether the inclusion of potentially omitted results would have an impact on the summary effect, especially for the comparison of TAAR1 agonists versus placebo in overall symptoms in acute schizophrenia at 3–13 weeks (see 6.1.1). This was carried out as part of the evaluation of biases due to missing evidence (see 10, 10.1, and 10.4.1).

There were in total 5 completed studies available for this comparison, with 4 presenting data that could be included in the meta-analysis, and one additional study [@sumitomo2024] that was terminated earlier after the first iteration of this review, enrolling 83 participants (see 10.1). The reason for the termination was company business strategy in clinicaltrials.gov, possibly based on the findings from the previous phase III trials (see 11.1). This study compared two doses of ulotaront (50 mg/day and 75 mg/day) with placebo for over 6 weeks, using a randomized double-blind design and a 1:1:1 ratio. Compared to the other included studies that were conducted in the USA and Europe, this trial was planned to be conducted across multiple sites in East Asia, including mainland China, Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines.

To assess the potential impact of including the omitted results from this study (sample size of 83 participants, 2:1 ratio of ulotaront to placebo) [@sumitomo2024] , we assumed a range of point estimates from –0.5 to 0.75. We calculated the corresponding standard error of each effect size based on the assumed point estimate, the total number of participants, and the allocation ratio, and then combined these with the findings from the other studies (see 6.1.1). Subsequently, we plotted the summary effects of these meta-analyses using both random- and fixed-effects models across the range of assumed point estimates for the study with omitted results [@sumitomo2024] .

```{r echo=F, fig.fullwidth=T, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, warning=FALSE}

data_available<-data.frame(study=meta_comp_overall_sch$studlab, TE=meta_comp_overall_sch$TE, seTE=meta_comp_overall_sch$seTE)

n=83 #the sample size of the missing study 
k=3 #n/k = the number of participants in the placebo group, so that n-n/k are the number of participants in teh ulotaront group  


j=1-3/(4*(n-2)-1) #J correction for Hedge's g 

data_sens_missing<-data.frame(es_missing=NA, 
                              TE.random=NA, ci.lb.random=NA, ci.ub.random=NA,
                              TE.fixed=NA, ci.lb.fixed=NA, ci.ub.fixed=NA)

for(es in seq(-0.50, 0.75, by=0.02)){
  d=es/j #Cohen's d from assumed es in Hedge's g 
  vd=((k^2)/(n*(k-1)))+((es^2)/(2*n)) # variance of cohen's d using the k and n of the study
  vj=(j^2)*vd #variance of Hedge's g
  seTE=sqrt(vj)
  
  data_missing<-data.frame(study="NCT04825860", TE=es, seTE=seTE)
  data_sens<-rbind(data_available, data_missing)
  
  meta_missing<-metagen(data=data_sens, TE=TE, seTE=seTE)
  
  data_sens_missing_i<-data.frame(es_missing=es, 
                                TE.random=meta_missing$TE.random,
                                ci.lb.random=meta_missing$TE.random-1.96*metagen(data=data_sens, TE=TE, seTE)$seTE.random,
                                ci.ub.random=meta_missing$TE.random+1.96*meta_missing$seTE.random,
                                TE.fixed=meta_missing$TE.fixed,
                                ci.lb.fixed=meta_missing$TE.fixed-1.96*meta_missing$seTE.fixed,
                                ci.ub.fixed=meta_missing$TE.fixed+1.96*meta_missing$seTE.fixed)
  
  data_sens_missing<-rbind(data_sens_missing, data_sens_missing_i)
  
}

ggplot(data = data_sens_missing, aes(x = es_missing)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ci.lb.random, ymax = ci.ub.random, fill="random"),  alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line( aes(y = TE.random, colour="random"))+
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ci.lb.fixed, ymax = ci.ub.fixed, fill="fixed"),   alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line( aes(y = TE.fixed, colour="fixed"))+
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(x = 0.80, y = meta_comp_overall_sch$TE.random, ymin = meta_comp_overall_sch$TE.random- 1.96*meta_comp_overall_sch$seTE.random, ymax =  meta_comp_overall_sch$TE.random+ 1.96*meta_comp_overall_sch$seTE.random, colour="random"),  size = 1) +
    geom_pointrange(aes(x = 0.85, y = meta_comp_overall_sch$TE.fixed, ymin = meta_comp_overall_sch$TE.fixed- 1.96*meta_comp_overall_sch$seTE.fixed, ymax =  meta_comp_overall_sch$TE.fixed+ 1.96*meta_comp_overall_sch$seTE.fixed, colour="fixed"), size = 1) +
  xlim(c(-0.45, 0.85))+
  ylim(c(-0.5, 0.85))+
    scale_color_manual(name = "Model", values = c("random" = "#00BFC4", "fixed" = "#F8766D")) +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Model", values = c("random" = "#00BFC4", "fixed" = "#F8766D")) +
  xlab("Assumed SMD of NCT04825860 to be included in the meta-analysis \n(SMD>0: TAAR1 agonists better to placebo)")+
  ylab("Summary effect (SMD 95%CI)")+
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.75, label = "Inclusion of omitted results \nfrom NCT04825860", hjust = 0, size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.8, y = 0.75, label = "Original", hjust = 0, size = 4) +
  theme_bw()


```

**Figure 97** Exploration of the potential impact of the omitted data from one study with unavailable results on the summary effect of the comparison of TAAR1 agonists vs. placebo on overall symptoms in acute schizophrenia at 3–13 weeks. The x-axis represents the point estimate of the SMD of the omitted results from [@sumitomo2024]. The y-axis represents the summary effects of a meta-analysis including the omitted results across the potential range of assumed effect sizes (from –0.5 to 0.75). The findings from the original meta-analysis without including the omitted results are also presented for comparison. The results from both the random- and fixed-effects models are shown.

It appears that the inclusion of the omitted results from [@sumitomo2024] would not have materially changed the summary effects in either the random- or fixed-effects meta-analysis. The findings were especially robust within the range of the most plausible effect sizes (e.g., between –0.2 and 0.4), with the point estimates of the meta-analysis falling within the range of trivial to small effects (e.g., between 0.10 and 0.17). Thus, it can be concluded that the omission of the results from [@sumitomo2024] would not have had a substantial impact on the summary effects of the meta-analysis for this comparison (see 10.4.1).

# 10. Risk of bias due to missing evidence

Risk of bias due to missing evidence was evaluated using the ROB-ME framework [@page2023], taking into account the usable data from the eligible studies identified through the search, the comprehensiveness of the search strategy, and potential patterns of missing data and small-study effects. We followed the ROB-ME algorithm to assign a judgment of low risk, high risk, or some concerns regarding reporting bias by systematically completing the steps and answering the signalling questions related to the relevant domains.

Specifically, the ROB-ME framework involves four steps in the assessment of reporting biases:

1.  Selecting and defining the meta-analysis to be assessed for reporting biases. We focused on the meta-analyses presented in the summary of evidence tables (see Section 11).

2.  Identifying studies that met the review’s eligibility criteria but had missing results, and assessing the reasons for missingness. These assessments are presented in the Results Matrix in Section 10.2, based on an adapted version of the ROB-ME framework.

3.  Assessing the potential for missing studies in the systematic review and the adequacy of the search strategy. This assessment is provided in Section 10.3.

4.  Assessing the risk of bias due to missing evidence by responding to signalling questions and applying the ROB-ME algorithm, incorporating the evaluations from the previous steps. The algorithm and the signalling questions is presented below in **Figure 91**.

```{r echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("data_u1/rob_me_step4.png")
```

## 10.1 Results matrix

We identified the total number of eligible and completed studies, with or without usable data, that could contribute to dropout and safety data for each comparison (as shown in **Table 1** and **Table 2**):

1.  TAAR1 agonists vs. placebo over a period of 1 day to 2 weeks: 13 studies with 661 participants.

2.  TAAR1 agonists vs. antipsychotics over a period of 1 day to 2 weeks: 2 studies with 100 participants.

3.  TAAR1 agonists vs. placebo for 3-13 weeks: 7 studies involving 1550 participants

    -   5 studies examining monotherapy for acute schizophrenia (4 with available data, and 1 without available data for the meta-analysis, see 9.3),

    -   1 study [@RN13] examning monotherapy for psychosis related to Parkinson's disease,

    -   1 study [@hoffmann-laroche2024] with two parts focusing on predominant negative symptoms and examining both monotherapy and adjunctive treatment to antipsychotics.

4.  TAAR1 agonists continuation vs. placebo discontinuation for 3-13 weeks: 1 study (NCT05848700) with 63 participants (the exact study duration is unclear, the study has been completed but no data available).

5.  TAAR1 agonists vs. antipsychotics for 3-13 weeks:

    -   1 study [@hoffmann-laroche2022] involving 214 participants in acute schizophrenia.

    -   1 study (NCT05542264) examining metabolic parameters in 19 clinically-stable participants with schizophrenia (the exact study duration is unclear, the study has been completed but no data available).

6.  TAAR1 agonists vs. antipsychotics for more than 13 weeks: 1 study [@nct04115319] with 303 participants.

## 10.2 Funnel plots and examination of small-study effects

There were insufficient data for the primary outcome but also other outcomes (i.e., fewer than 10 studies) to examine small-study effects with funnel plots. Thus, we cannot explore the pattern of missing evidence or conduct sensitivity analysis to explore the potential impact of the missing evidence.

Thus, we replied accordingly to the following signalling questions:

-   ROB-ME-4.7 ("*Does the pattern of observed study results suggest that the meta-analysis is likely to be missing results that were systematically different (in terms of P value, magnitude or direction) from those observed?*") - "probably no", as no pattern can be observed due to the small number of available studies, but all studies should have been identified.

-   ROB-ME-4.8 ("*Did sensitivity analyses suggest that the summary effect estimate was biased due to missing results?*") - "not applicable", as no sensitivity analysis was conducted.

## 10.3 Coverage of the search strategy

We conducted a comprehensive search for both published and unpublished studies in multiple electronic databases, supplemented by manual searches of the reference lists of included studies and previous reviews. Screening was carried out by at least two independent reviewers.

Potential limitations of the search strategy:

-   All studies identified in the search were conducted by the pharmaceutical industry. Although we contacted them, we have not received additional data for the first and second iteration. Considering that all eligible studies are experimental and were conducted recently, it is expected that most, if not all, have been registered, thus facilitating their detection during searches in clinical trial registries. Nonetheless, it's possible that small phase I studies focusing on pharmacokinetics may not have been registered and could therefore have been overlooked. Consequently, we do not anticipate that our search has missed any major or significant studies.

-   The search strategies used in the first and second iterations of the review were designed to identify studies of newly synthesized drugs with a primary mechanism of action as TAAR1 agonists. However, an increasing number of older drugs have since been identified as TAAR1 agonists, and these were not captured by the current search strategies. Nonetheless, the potential reporting biases associated with these older drugs are likely to stem from different reasons. Therefore, we anticipate that the current assessment, which focuses on newer compounds, would not have been meaningfully affected by this omission of the older compounds.

It should be noted that one unpublished ralmitaront RCT on PET measures [@pet_ralmitaront] was identified in the updated searches as a retrospectively registered study on ClinicalTrials.gov. However, this may not raise further concerns about the comprehensiveness of the search strategy.

Thus, we replied accordingly to the following signalling questions:

-   ROB-ME-3.1 ("*Were prospectively registered studies or studies identified for a prospective meta-analysis the only type of study eligible for inclusion in the review?*") - "no".

-   ROB-ME-3.2 ("*Would you expect every eligible study to be identifiable regardless of its results?*") - "probably yes".

-   ROB-ME-3.3 ("*Were you likely to have found all eligible studies regardless of their results?*") - "probably yes".

-   ROB-ME-4.5 ("*Do circumstances (identified in Step 3) indicate potential for some eligible studies not being identified because of the P value, magnitude or direction of the results generated?*") - "no".

## 10.4 ROB-ME evaluation

### 10.4.1 Reporting bias assessment for efficacy outcomes

We conducted the ROB-ME evaluation for the efficacy outcomes (primary and secondary) by examining the comparisons within each population separately.

#### Primary outcome

The availability of data for the primary outcome varied across comparisons and populations.

For the comparison of *TAAR1 agonists versus placebo as monotherapy in acute schizophrenia,* five studies were eligible: data were available from four studies, while one study, which was terminated early [@sumitomo2024], did not provide data (see 10.1). A sensitivity analysis found that omitting the findings of the latter study would not have an important impact on the summary of effects (see 9.3).

Thus, we responded accordingly to the following signalling questions, which led to a judgment of *low risk of reporting bias,* in line with the ROB-ME algorithm (see Figure 93) and taking into account the comprehensiveness of the search strategy (see 10.3):

-   ROB-ME-4.1 ("*Of the studies identified, was there any for which no result was available for inclusion in the meta-analysis, likely because of the P value, magnitude or direction of the result generated (refer to Step 2)*?) - "yes"

-   ROB-ME-4.2 ("*Is it likely that there would be a notable change to the summary effect estimate if the omitted results had been included?*") - "no"

-   ROB-ME-4.3 ("*Of the studies identified, was there any for which it was unclear whether an eligible result was generated (refer to Step 2)?*" - "yes", as the study [@RN112] consisted of two parts—one for adults and one for adolescents—but for the latter, it is unclear whether an eligible result was generated.

-   ROB-ME-4.4 ("Is it likely that there would be a notable change to the summary effect estimate if the potentially omitted results had been included?") - "no information", as it was unclear the sample size of the adolescent participants, if recruited.

For the comparisons of *TAAR1 agonists vs. placebo in Parkinson's disease psychosis, TAAR1 agonists vs. antipsychotics in acute schizophrenia*, and T*AAR1 agonists vs. placebo (as monotherapy or add-on) in participants with schizophrenia and predominant negative symptoms*, one study was eligible for each analysis. Therefore, following a similar approach as described above, a *low risk of reporting bias* was assigned.

No data were available from eligible studies for the comparison of TAAR1 agonists versus placebo or antipsychotics in patients with clinically stable schizophrenia, or for timepoints other than 3 to 13 weeks.

#### Secondary efficacy outcomes

For the *comparison of TAAR1 agonists versus placebo*, there were 5 studies eligible as mentioned in 10.4.1. with varied availability in the data for the secondary efficacy outcomes:

-   We assigned a *low risk of reporting bias* for the outome of response to treatment similar to the primary outcome of overall symptoms (see 10.4.1).

-   The two failed phase III trials[@RN111; @RN112] did not report effects on specific symptoms (e.g., positive, negative, and depressive symptoms). It is likely that the inclusion of these omitted results would have impacted the summary estimates, introducing a bias in favor of TAAR1 agonists. Additionally, the prematurely terminated trial [@sumitomo2024] also lacked available data. Consequently, these analyses are at risk of bias due to missing evidence, and we assigned a high risk of reporting bias (ROB-ME-4.1 "yes", ROB-ME-4.2 "yes").

For the comparisons of *TAAR1 agonists vs. placebo in Parkinson's disease psychosis, TAAR1 agonists vs. antipsychotics in acute schizophrenia*, and T*AAR1 agonists vs. placebo (as monotherapy or add-on) in participants with schizophrenia and predominant negative symptoms*, *TAAR1 agonists vs. antipsychotics in clinically stable schizophrenia (1 day to 2 weeks, and \>13 weeks)*, one study was eligible for each analysis. Therefore, following a similar approach as described above, a *low risk of reporting bias* was assigned.

No data were available from eligible studies for other comparisons or for timepoints except 3-13 weeks (except for the cases mentioned above).

### 10.4.2 Reporting bias assessment for the secondary acceptability and tolerability outcomes

We conducted the ROB-ME evaluation for acceptability and tolerability outcomes (i.e., dropouts and side effects) by examining comparisons that pooled the different populations, in accordance with the analyses presented above.

The reasons for missing data on these outcomes are often unclear. In most cases, the data were either not measured or not reported for reasons unrelated to the P-values, effect sizes, or direction of effects—although selective non-reporting based on such factors cannot be entirely ruled out.

Therefore, we employed, as a general rule, the following approach to respond to the signalling questions of ROB-ME:

-   ROB-ME-4.1 "no", as no result was generally considered to have been omitted for these outcomes due to their P-value, magnitude, or direction (see 10.1 and **Table 2**). Thus, ROB-ME-4.2 is "not applicable".

-   ROB-ME-4.3 "yes" because there were studies for which it was unclear whether results for these outcomes were generated (see 10.1 and **Table 2**).

-   ROB-ME-4.4

    -   'no information" if there were data from less than 50% of the participants of the total sample of the eligible studies, suggesting the possibility that the findings could notably change if the missing data had been added to the analysis. The cut-off of 50% of the participants was selected to balance out the fact that, in most cases, the findings were not missing due to unfavorable results (see Table 2), but also to consider the possibility that the findings may be likely to change with the addition of missing evidence, given the small number of studies and participants contributing to the estimates.

    -   "probably no" if data were available from more than 50% of the participants in the total sample of the eligible studies.

Thus, we assigned some concerns or a *moderate risk of bias* due to missing evidence when ROB-ME-4.4 was rated as "no information", and a *low risk* when ROB-ME-4.4 was rated as "probably no" (considering ROB-ME-4.5 "no," ROB-ME-4.7 "no," and ROB-ME-4.8 "no"; see Sections 10.2, 10.3, and Figure 93).

### 10.4.4 Reporting bias assessment for mechanistic insights

We assigned a *high risk* of reporting bias for outcomes related to mechanistic insights (F-DOPA PET and fMRI). This judgment was based on the identification of a new ralmitaront RCT [@pet_ralmitaront] in the search, which had unavailable results and was retrospectively registered, indicating that the findings may not have been published due to the magnitude, direction, or statistical significance of the results, although this remains uncertain. The study had a double-blind, crossover design and included 35 participants with clinically stable schizophrenia. Potential negative findings from this study could potentially have an impact on the results, given that only one small study contributed data to the each of the fMRI and PET outcomes. (ROB-ME-4.1 “yes”; ROB-ME-4.2 “yes”). The search was comprehensive, and no other studies assessing neurobiological outcomes are expected to have been eligible.

# 11. Summary of evidence

## 11.1 Approach to evaluate the confidence in the evidence

For each comparison, outcome and timepoint, we presented the summary of the evidence by presenting the summary of the association, biases due to study limitations, biases due to reporting bias, biases due to indirectness and other biases.

### 11.1.1 Summary of the association

We presented the number of studies (N), participants (n) contributing to the analysis, the point estimates and 95% confidence intervals for both random- and fixed-effects models. We also made a statement about dose-effects for the primary outcome (see 8.4).

### 11.1.2 Within-study biases

This refers to the study limitations assessed using the risk of bias tool RoB2 [@RN64] (see 5. and **Figure 2**). The majority of studies had a low risk of bias or, at most, some concerns across domains, mainly related to missing outcome data, and in some cases to the randomization process, period and carry-over effects [@RN124; @milanovic2024], and deviations from the intended intervention [@milanovic2024]) and across outcomes. The exception was three studies [@RN13; @hoffmann-laroche2024; @otsukapharmaceuticaldevelopmentcommercializationinc2024], which were rated as having a high risk of bias due to missing outcome data and thus an overall high risk of bias for the efficacy outcomes.

Thus, for within-study biases, we assigned:

-   "High risk" when the efficacy outcomes were based solely on studies with an overall high risk of bias [@RN13; @hoffmann-laroche2024; @otsukapharmaceuticaldevelopmentcommercializationinc2024].

-   "Low risk" when the included studies had a low risk or at most some concerns, mainly in the domain of missing outcome data, and no more than 50% of the studies were assigned an overall judgement of some concerns.

-   "Moderate risk" when the included studies had a low risk or at most some concerns, mainly in the domain of missing outcome data, but more than 50% of the studies were assigned an overall judgement of some concerns.

The justification was that, in most cases, some concerns were raised due to missing outcome data. A recent meta-epidemiological study suggested that biases due to missing outcome data might underestimate the effects [@wang2024]. In schizophrenia trials, there is evidence that participants who dropped out may have a worse prognosis compared to those who stayed in the trial [@rabinowitz2008]. However, there were generally no clear differences in dropouts between TAAR1 agonists and control conditions, although TAAR1 may be associated with higher dropout rates compared to placebo (**Figure 11**). Therefore, we judged that a high risk of bias due to missing outcome data in efficacy outcomes in @RN13 and @hoffmann-laroche2024 could have possibly overestimated the effects of TAAR1 agonists compared to placebo in favor of the former. However, in other cases, when there were some concerns for safety, it is unclear whether missing outcome data could have led to biased findings. The same rationale was applied to the outcome of relapse, as it was often either a reason for dropout or defined as an adverse event.

Other domains of bias, such as bias due to randomization in a crossover trial [@RN124], potential biases due to period and carry-over effects in two studies [@RN124; @milanovic2024] , and due to deviations from intended intervention and outcome measurement in one open trial [@milanovic2024], were also considered, mainly within the overall judgment of potential risk of bias, and potentially in favor of the experimental intervention of TAAR1 agonists.

### 11.1.3 Across-study bias

This is referring to risk of bias due to missing evidence, and we used the approach mentioned above to assign "low risk", "moderate risk" or "high risk" (see more details in section 10).

### 11.1.4 Indirectness

We assessed the potential indirectness of the findings by taking into consideration the characteristics of the population, intervention, control conditions, outcomes, and settings of the clinical trials. It should be noted that our focus was primarily on clinical trial settings, rather than on the generalizability of the findings to real-world populations. The main population to which the findings will be applied is people with schizophrenia and other schizophrenia-like conditions, unless a specific analysis was conducted for a different subgroup (e.g., as for efficacy outcomes).

For efficacy outcomes, we assigned a "low risk" of indirectness, as we conducted separate analyses for the different subpopulations and found no concerns regarding population, interventions, control conditions, outcomes, or settings in the eligible trials. For relapse, we assigned a "moderate risk" of indirectness when the outcome was defined as a "schizophrenia" adverse event in one study [@otsukapharmaceuticaldevelopmentcommercializationinc2024] rather than dropouts due to relapse or using other operationalized definitions of relapse.

For safety and acceptability outcomes, potential indirectness in terms of population characteristics may exist in the analysis of the acceptability and tolerability outcomes. This is because we pooled data from diverse populations, including those with schizophrenia spectrum disorders, Parkinson's disease psychosis, narcolepsy-cataplexy, and healthy volunteers. Thus, we assigned:

-   "Moderate risk" when fewer than 50% of participants in the analysis were people with schizophrenia or schizophrenia-like conditions.

-   "Low risk" when the analysis included at least 50% of the participants in the analysis were people with schizophrenia or schizophrenia-like conditions.

Nevertheless, the impact on the magnitude and direction of the effects remains unclear.

### 11.1.5 Other biases

We considered additional biases, such as potential factors that could impact the magnitude and direction of the findings.

We assigned a "moderate risk" of other biases for the primary outcomes of overall symptoms and response to treatment in the comparison of TAAR1 agonists versus placebo in adults experiencing an acute episode of schizophrenia. This was due to potential concerns in the two phase III trials on ulotaront, which were associated with high placebo responses and reduced assay sensitivity [@RN111; @RN112]. The following reasons are described:

-   High placebo responses—of approximately 14 and 19 points average reduction in PANSS total scores from baseline—were observed in these two trials  [@RN111; @RN112] . To put this into context, the average reduction in PANSS total scores in antipsychotic trials is approximately 6 points, although larger reductions have been reported in more recent trials [@leucht2018], and an average reduction of 9.7 points in PANSS total scores in the placebo group of the in the phase II ulotaront trial  [@RN110]. This suggests that potential factors associated with elevated placebo responses could have diluted the effect sizes and led to an underestimation of the treatment effects.

-   The potential underlying reasons and impact of the high placebo responses were explored in additional analyses, as reported in conference abstracts from ACNP 2024 [@RN109] and SIRS 2024.

    A pre-specified analysis that pooled participants of the two phase III trials [@RN111; @RN112] enrolled before the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic found smaller placebo responses and effect sizes similar to those observed in the phase II trial of ulotaront @RN110, i.e., –15.8 points reduction in the ulotaront 50–100 mg/day group vs. –8.8 points in the placebo group; p=0.017, SMD=0.47. In contrast, no difference between the groups was observed among participants enrolled after the onset of COVID-19. Based on the data presented above, it can be estimated that 10-15% of the total sample size consisted of participants enrolled before the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.

    Possible explanations included regional differences—most pre-pandemic participants were enrolled in the US—and the initiation or dose increase of antipsychotic medication shortly before study entry, which may have contributed to higher placebo responses and reduced separation between ulotaront and placebo. Other contributing factors may include recruitment pressure during the pandemic, which could have led to baseline score inflation and less careful participant selection, as well as difficulties in trial execution and monitoring, such as protocol deviations and co-treatments [@leucht2013; @leucht2019].

    It should be noted that another trial was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic [@RN113], but the potential impact of the pandemic on its execution has not been reported. Nonetheless, the possibility that the observed findings may underestimate the true effect cannot be excluded.

No other biases were identified for almost all comparisons and outcomes.

### 11.2.4 Mechanistic insights of TAAR1 agonism for psychosis

Evidence from two neuroimaging studies [@RN115; @RN132] generally supports the notion that TAAR1 agonists can ameliorate the elevated striatal dopamine synthesis and release capacity that is considered central in the development of symptoms of psychosis [@howes2022]. The summary of the evidence of these studies is presented below. It should be noted that another study [@pet_ralmitaront], identified in the updated searches, remains unpublished and was retrospectively registered on ClinicalTrials.gov.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}
knitr::kable(soe_mechanistic)
```

**Table 11** Summary of evidence table for the mechanistic insights of TAAR1 agonism for psychosis. The findings of two studies [@RN115; @RN132] with available neurobiological measures relevant to psychosis are narratively reported. These include the double-blind randomized controlled trial of @RN115 with the fMRI BOLD striatal responses in the anticipatory phase of the Monetary Incentive Delay (MID) task (proxy for increased dopaminergic signalling in the striatum), and the open label single-arm study of @RN132 with F-DOPA PET in the striatum. Across-study bias was evaluated using the ROB-ME approach [@page2023]. N=number of studies, n=number of participants. SMD=Standardized mean difference, 95%CI: 95% confidence interval. p-value: p-value for the correlation coefficient.
